name: Project Juniper
one_liner: Split one corporate workstation into two isolated operating systems: an open one for the internet and a locked one for sensitive enterprise access.

buyer.company_profile: Large regulated enterprises (banks, financial services, technology vendors) that today lock down endpoints or issue two laptops to privileged users.

user: Employees with privileged or sensitive access (IT admins, finance, traders, developers) and the desktop teams who manage their machines.

problem.summary: Enterprises lock down devices (no free browsing, app installs, USB or cloud use), frustrating employees and hurting productivity, or adopt an air-gap model where privileged users carry two laptops. Both are costly. Approaches that rely on the security of a single vulnerable operating system fail when users are tricked into running malware or a zero-day is exploited.

evidence.claim: Air-gapping separates sensitive systems from untrusted networks, at the cost of usability.
Hypervisors can run multiple isolated operating systems on one machine.
Security-focused desktop systems use virtualisation to compartmentalise untrusted activity.
Privileged access workstations are recommended for administrators to reduce credential theft risk.

why_now.summary: Hardware virtualisation support is standard on corporate laptops, making it practical to run two isolated OSes side by side with a seamless user experience; targeted phishing and zero-days make single-OS hardening insufficient.

features.feature: Thin hypervisor that runs a locked corporate OS and an unrestricted OS side by side
features.why: Malware in one OS cannot reach the other.

features.feature: Seamless window integration so users see one desktop
features.why: Avoid the usability cost of two laptops.

features.feature: Central management of both OS images and policies
Controlled data transfer between the two sides

competitors.name: Bromium
competitors.how_we_differ: Isolates the whole sensitive environment, not individual tasks.

competitors.name: VMware Horizon (VDI)
competitors.how_we_differ: Local execution with offline use and no data-centre VDI cost.

competitors.name: Menlo Security (browser isolation)
competitors.how_we_differ: Covers all untrusted activity (apps, USB), not only the browser.

competitors.name: Two physical laptops / privileged access workstations
Qubes OS (free, open source)
competitors.how_we_differ: Enterprise-manageable Windows experience rather than an expert Linux desktop.

differentiation: Security by architecture rather than detection: two fully isolated OSes on one workstation, so users get freedom on one side while the corporate side stays locked; cheaper than two laptops or VDI, and stronger than single-OS hardening.

build.team: About 20 people: virtualisation and security engineers, with founders from elite military cyber units and enterprise security sales
hardest_parts: Hypervisor compatibility across hardware and Windows versions
Performance and battery life on laptops
Fitting into existing endpoint management tooling

pricing.entry_price: Working assumption: $200 per endpoint per year, 500-endpoint minimum
pricing.rationale: Priced well below the cost of a second laptop or a VDI seat.

comparables.price: No public list price at the time (quote-based enterprise sale)
No public list price at the time (quote-based enterprise sale)

go_to_market.first_customers: Ten large banks, financial services firms and technology vendors that already issue separate devices to administrators or restrict internet access.
go_to_market.channel: Direct enterprise sales leveraging investor and founder networks with large-company CISOs.
go_to_market.wedge: Privileged IT administrators who today carry two laptops.

risks: Operating-system vendors build similar isolation natively
Long enterprise sales cycles for endpoint architecture changes

riskiest_assumption.assumption: Enterprises will replace locked-down or dual-device setups with a two-OS workstation at fleet scale.
riskiest_assumption.test: Interview 10 enterprise desktop/infra leads about current dual-device cost and willingness to pilot on 50 privileged users.
riskiest_assumption.success_signal: At least 4 of 10 commit to a paid pilot with budget identified.

open_questions: Does value extend beyond privileged users to the whole workforce?
How will this coexist with endpoint agents and management tools?
